AFRICAE.

in the middle of the area, where the prefect of the moneyers sits, who is perpetually attended by scribes and notaries. For here, as in many other places, whatever profit is collected returns entirely to the King. Adjacent to this place are the workshops of the goldsmiths, whose consul keeps the seal and the dies for the coins. In Fez, neither a ring nor any other object may be manufactured from gold or silver unless the metal has first been sealed: for they punish offenders with the utmost severity. Once the metal is sealed, however, whatever is crafted from it is spent just as if it were coin. The greater part of the goldsmiths who inhabit the new city of Fez consists of Jews, and they carry their gold and silver vessels to a certain place in the old city of Fez, located not far from the spice merchants, to sell them. For in old Fez, neither gold nor silver is minted, nor are the <term>Mahumetani</term> <gloss>Muslims</gloss> permitted to practice that craft, because they [the Muslims] have usurers [among them] who resell any silver or gold work at a higher price than the weight warrants, although this is permitted to the Jews by the city governors. You may also find here some who only fashion vessels for the citizens, for which they are paid only according to the measure of their labor. <summary>This passage describes the regulation of precious metals in Fez, noting the strict control over goldsmiths and the role of the Jewish community in the trade of manufactured gold and silver goods.</summary>
